expectedText:
INDIVIDUAL HEALTH CARE INSTRUCTION
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · I do not want my life to be prolonged if I have an incurable and irreversible condition with no reasonable chance of recovery

DECLARATION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, being an adult of sound mind, give this individual health care instruction to make known my wishes regarding my own health care. I am not naming an agent or granting anyone power of attorney for health care in this document. I revoke any prior individual health care instruction I have made that is inconsistent with this one.

THE STATUTORY BASIS FOR A STAND-ALONE INSTRUCTION
An adult having capacity to make health care decisions may give an individual health care instruction directly, without executing a power of attorney for health care or naming any health care agent. Jordan Alex Lee's instruction may be oral or written, and may be limited to take effect only if a specified condition arises. California's Health Care Decisions Law treats this individual health care instruction as one of exactly two forms an advance health care directive can take — the other being a power of attorney for health care that appoints an agent — and a person may use either form alone, or combine both in one document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An adult having capacity may give an individual health care instruction. The individual instruction may be oral or written. The individual instruction may be limited to take effect only if a specified condition arises."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4670, an adult may give an individual health care instruction without an agent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4670.)
  ""Advance health care directive" or "advance directive" means either an individual health care instruction or a power of attorney for health care."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4605, definition of advance health care directive as either component (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4605.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a stand-alone instruction with no named agent is its own recognized category under this state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. Cal. Prob. Code § 4605 is the same definitional provision already cited in this project's Advance Health Care Directive document; it is cited again here only to show where a stand-alone instruction sits within that same two-part statutory structure, not as an independent new source for that structural point.

WHAT AN INSTRUCTION IS FOR, AND WHAT IT CAN ADDRESS
The Legislature has found that an adult has the fundamental right to control decisions relating to their own health care, including the decision to have life-sustaining treatment withheld or withdrawn, and that prolonging the dying process for someone whose prognosis cannot be improved may cause needless pain and suffering without medical benefit. Consistent with that, an individual health care instruction can address the same broad range of health care decisions the statute recognizes: selection and discharge of health care providers and institutions; approval or disapproval of diagnostic tests, surgical procedures, and medication (including for mental health conditions); and directions to provide, withhold, or withdraw artificial nutrition and hydration and all other forms of health care, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) In recognition of the dignity and privacy a person has a right to expect, the law recognizes that an adult has the fundamental right to control the decisions relating to his or her own health care, including the decision to have life-sustaining treatment withheld or withdrawn. (b) Modern medical technology has made possible the artificial prolongation of human life beyond natural limits. In the interest of protecting individual autonomy, this prolongation of the process of dying for a person for whom continued health care does not improve the prognosis for recovery may violate patient dignity and cause unnecessary pain and suffering, while providing nothing medically necessary or beneficial to the person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4650(a)-(b), legislative findings on the right to refuse life-sustaining treatment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4650.)
  ""Health care decision" means a decision made by a patient or the patient's agent, conservator, or surrogate, regarding the patient's health care, including the following: (1) Selection and discharge of health care providers and institutions. (2) Approval or disapproval of diagnostic tests, surgical procedures, and programs of medication, including mental health conditions. (3) Directions to provide, withhold, or withdraw artificial nutrition and hydration and all other forms of health care, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4617(a), the defined scope of health care decisions an instruction can address (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4617.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the Legislature's own stated purpose and of the actual breadth of subject matter an instruction can cover — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. § 4617 defines "health care decision" generally rather than "individual health care instruction" specifically; it is used here because an instruction operates by directing decisions within that same defined scope.

MY INSTRUCTIONS
Regarding treatment intended to prolong my life: I do not want my life to be prolonged if I have an incurable and irreversible condition with no reasonable chance of recovery. Regarding relief from pain or discomfort: I want treatment for alleviation of pain, even if it hastens my death. Additional instructions regarding my physical or mental health care: Any other wishes about your physical or mental health care. This instruction takes effect Immediately upon execution.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM AN AHCD WITH AN AGENT: NO ONE INTERPRETS IT, A PROVIDER MUST FOLLOW IT DIRECTLY
Unlike a power of attorney for health care, an individual health care instruction does not appoint anyone to interpret it or to act on Jordan Alex Lee's behalf. That absence of an agent does not weaken the instruction: a health care provider or health care institution treating Jordan Alex Lee must comply directly with Jordan Alex Lee's individual health care instruction, and — separately, if someone is then authorized to make health care decisions for Jordan Alex Lee, such as an agent, surrogate, or conservator — must also comply with that person's reasonable interpretation of the instruction. The instruction is binding on its own; a named agent is not required to make it enforceable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An adult having capacity may execute a power of attorney for health care, as provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 4680). The power of attorney for health care may authorize the agent to make health care decisions and may also include individual health care instructions."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4671(a), contrast: a power of attorney for health care requires executing an agent-appointment instrument (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4671.)
  "Except as provided in Sections 4734 and 4735, a health care provider or health care institution providing care to a patient shall do the following: (a) Comply with an individual health care instruction of the patient and with a reasonable interpretation of that instruction made by a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4733(a), a provider's duty to comply with the instruction itself, independent of any interpreter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4733.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how an instruction operates without a named agent — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. The remainder of this compliance duty — its conscience-based and medically-ineffective-treatment exceptions, and the provider's notify-and-transfer obligation when it declines — is the identical duty already fully covered by this project's Advance Health Care Directive document (Cal. Prob. Code §§ 4734-4736); it is not re-derived here.

ORAL INSTRUCTIONS NEED NO FORMALITY; WRITTEN ONES FOLLOW THE SAME RULES AS ANY WRITTEN DIRECTIVE
An individual health care instruction may be given orally, with no signing, dating, witnessing, or notarization of any kind. If Jordan Alex Lee instead chooses to put the instruction in writing, that writing is a written advance health care directive and must meet the same legal-sufficiency requirements as any other one — it must state its execution date, be signed by Jordan Alex Lee (or by another adult in Jordan Alex Lee's presence and at Jordan Alex Lee's direction), and be either notarized or signed by two qualifying witnesses. Those execution and witness-disqualification rules are already covered by this project's Advance Health Care Directive document and are not repeated here; this document exists specifically for the oral-or-simple-written case where no agent is being named.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An adult having capacity may give an individual health care instruction. The individual instruction may be oral or written. The individual instruction may be limited to take effect only if a specified condition arises."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4670 [oral or written], an instruction may be oral or written (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4670.)
  "A written advance health care directive is legally sufficient if all of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) The advance directive contains the date of its execution. (2) The advance directive is signed either by the patient or in the patient's name by another adult in the patient's presence and at the patient's direction. (3) The advance directive is either acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two witnesses who satisfy the requirements of Sections 4674 and 4675."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4673(a), legal sufficiency requirements that apply once an instruction is put in writing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4673.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an oral instruction requires no formality at all, in contrast to a written one — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. The written-form execution requirement cited here (§ 4673(a)) is the same rule already fully quoted in this project's ahcd_execution_requirements clause; it is cited again only to establish that it applies identically to a written individual instruction, and is not a new or independent finding about that rule's content.

REVOKING THIS INSTRUCTION IS ALWAYS THE EASIER STANDARD
While having capacity, Jordan Alex Lee may revoke this individual health care instruction, in whole or in part, at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke — no signed writing is required. Because this document names no agent, none of it is ever subject to the stricter signed-writing-or-personal-notice rule that California law reserves specifically for revoking an agent designation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A patient having capacity may revoke all or part of an advance health care directive, other than the designation of an agent, at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4695(b), the looser revocation method for anything other than an agent designation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4695.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, looser revocation standard that applies to an instruction with no agent to designate or un-designate — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4695(b)); the stricter agent-revocation subsection, § 4695(a), is already covered by this project's ahcd_revocation clause and does not apply to this document because it names no agent.

SIGNATURE (IF IN WRITING)
This instruction may be given orally and need not be signed at all. If it is put in writing, as here, it should be signed and dated, and either notarized or signed by two qualifying witnesses, in the same manner as any other written advance health care directive.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________
